abstract: Motivated by issues of the maintenance of genetic variation in a highly endangered species, we continue earlier studies into the population genetics ancestry and descent of genome segments. In this paper, we focus on the survival and descent of genome in a population pedigree of a diploid dioecious species. We consider a population potentially being maintained from a small founder base, taking the canonical example a random-mating population of 100 males and 100 females. We show how previous methods to examine the ancestry of a single genome in such a population can also be used to account the survival genetic lengths and number of descendant copies of founder genome segments, and explore the variance of these measures. We show the variance of the population distribution over realizations within a pedigree is scarcely smaller then the variance over pedigrees: variation is in meiosis rather than in pedigree. While all founders continue to lose genome over time, the very first generations are critical to determining the amount of surviving genome. Dependence among founders is slight, except for between the two genomes of a founder: however when monogamy is enforced this high dependence extends to founder mates. We briefly consider extensions of population size (both smaller and larger), of mating structure, and of variance in offspring number, including variance in male reproductive success.
